The Central Intelligence Agency has previously admitted to using waterboarding on three individuals [File: Carolyn Kaster/AP Photo]By Brian OsgoodPublished On 26 Nov 202626 Nov 2026
The New York Times has reported that the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) may have waterboarded more people than it previously admitted.
Wednesday’s report comes after the newspaper filed a lawsuit to obtain material gathered by special prosecutor John Durham, who was appointed in 2008 to investigate the CIA’s activities.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3‘War on terror’: How 9/11 changed the language of conflictlist 2 of 3Rubio calls on Cubans to partner with CIA ‘to create positive change’list 3 of 3Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strikeend of list
Durham’s probe ended without any criminal charges. But The New York Times obtained partially redacted documents from his investigation, including a summary of a 2012 interview with an interpreter who described a previously unconfirmed act of waterboarding.
The account sheds new light on one of the most infamous methods of torture utilised by the intelligence agency after the attacks on September 11, 2001.
Waterboarding involves restraining a person and pouring water on their face through a cloth, to mimic the experience of drowning.
The CIA called the practice an “enhanced interrogation technique”. As part of the US’s so-called “war on terror”, the agency sent suspects to overseas prisons, known as black sites, where they would be tortured in secret, including through waterboarding.
While the practice was shielded from scrutiny for years, a 2009 executive order eventually barred continued waterboarding. Congress has likewise passed restrictions.

People stand next to the wreckage of vehicles in the aftermath of a fire that broke out in the Al-Waraq neighbourhood of Imbaba district, Giza Governorate [AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP, AP and ReutersPublished On 26 Nov 202626 Nov 2026
Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people.
The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.

The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.
In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.

An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy.

The Mexican government is seeking talks with aviation authorities in the United States about falling rocket debris following SpaceX launches in Texas.
It is the latest sign of growing tensions between Mexico City and Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company.

“What we are seeking, through the embassy, is a meeting between US and Mexican airspace authorities so that permission for the use of Mexican airspace can be established, how often it would be used, and, if necessary, the relocation of the launch site,” Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Thursday at a news conference in the capital.
“And then there’s the ⁠⁠⁠⁠issue of the debris,” she added.
Earlier this month, Mexican authorities said they had to recover debris after a launch of a SpaceX Starship from its Starbase,Texas, facility near the Gulf of Mexico and nature reserves on both sides of the shared border.
Debris that officials said came from the launch washed ashore along Playa Bagdad in Matamoros in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, according to PROFEPA, Mexico’s Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection.

Displaced Palestinians attempt to clear a water puddle outside their flooded tents amid heavy rainfall in Gaza [Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 26 Nov 202626 Nov 2026
When heavy rain swept through az-Zawayda in central Gaza in early November, water rushed into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent, soaking his family’s mattresses and spoiling their food.
Al-Kaseeh, who fled Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, told Al Jazeera that his camp had flooded three or four times the previous winter. Those floods had already driven many of his neighbours away.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Gaza’s infrastructure collapse leaves residents defenceless against floodslist 2 of 3Israel restricting treatment for 1,100 child amputees in Gaza: NGOlist 3 of 3Gaza meningitis cases surge as collapsing infrastructure fuels health fearsend of list
About 1.36 million Palestinians, 65 percent of Gaza’s population, are living in tents and makeshift shelters, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
The storm that began on the evening of November 6 flooded about 70,000 tents within 12 hours, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Preliminary UN estimates suggest it affected about 226,000 people, including more than 5,000 households left sleeping without shelter. About 600 households were forced to move again.
The rain also killed people. On November 8, a sand embankment collapsed onto tents at a displacement camp south of Deir el-Balah, killing five people, including children. OCHA reported that an infant drowned during the same storm and a nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on November 13.

US President Donald Trump - seen with Stephen Miller, now the White House chief of staff - signs executive orders related to birthright citizenship on August 6, 2026 [Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters]By Umar Farooq and ReutersPublished On 26 Nov 202626 Nov 2026
A United States federal judge has blocked an attempt by President Donald Trump’s administration to deny birthright citizenship to certain categories of US-born children whose parents it argued were not subject to US jurisdiction.
In a ruling issued on Wednesday, District Court Judge Christopher Cooper said those children were still under US jurisdiction and thus were guaranteed citizenship under the US Constitution.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3US judge denies injunction against Trump’s new birthright citizenship orderlist 2 of 3US Supreme Court rules against Trump order to end birthright citizenshiplist 3 of 3Trump signs new executive orders seeking to limit US birthright citizenshipend of list
“The president cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws,” Cooper said in the order.
Another court in Maryland had also blocked the same policy by the Trump administration in a September ruling, issuing a preliminary injunction at the time.
The new ruling is another blow to Trump’s campaign to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents at their birth.
